title: {{NAME}} and the Green Guard
moral: The world needs heroes who protect the small and quiet things, not just the large and loud ones.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a leafy-green hero suit with silver wing details, dark trousers, and forest-green boots — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
{{NAME}}'s hero name was Greenwatch, and his self-assigned mission was: urban nature.

Not the big exciting emergencies. The overlooked ones: the starling flock disrupted by construction, the bee colony in the condemned building, the river otter family cut off from the water by a new fence.

Nobody gave him credit for these.

He was okay with that.

Then the Thornwood Fairy Council contacted him and said: something bigger is coming.

pages.content:
The something bigger: a development company had acquired all the land around the Thornwood, a fifty-acre urban forest full of fairy settlements and established animal communities. Groundbreaking was in three days.

The Fairy Council had tried legal channels. The city records had tried. The animals had tried their own methods, which had been ineffective but creative.

{{NAME}} listened to the full briefing, which took two hours because every fairy had a different account of the same events and all of them had to be heard.

"What do you actually need from me?" he asked at the end.

"Documentation," said the head fairy. "Nobody knows what's in the wood."

pages.content:
He spent two days in the Thornwood, documenting everything: every fairy settlement, every animal family, every protected plant species, with photographs and notes and maps.

The fox guided him through the densest parts. The badger showed him the ancient set that had been occupied continuously for sixty years. The fairy council illuminated sections of the canopy nobody had mapped before.

He found three species that should have been on the protected list but weren't, because nobody had looked.

He filed the documentation that evening.

pages.content:
The development was halted the following day, pending environmental review.

The review would take months. The protected species listing would take weeks. Combined: the Thornwood was safe for at least a year, probably longer.

{{NAME}} stood at the Thornwood entrance as the review notice went up on the gate.

Every fairy in the wood came to the edge and hovered in a line.

The fox sat beside him.

The head fairy said, very formally: "The Thornwood recognises Greenwatch as a friend."

{{NAME}} didn't say anything, because there wasn't anything that needed saying.

pages.content:
He walked home through the city in his hero suit, the documentation folder under his arm.

The city moved around him: busy and loud and entirely unaware of what had just been saved.

He thought: most heroism looks like this. Paperwork and patience and showing up when nobody is watching.

In bed, he lay looking at the ceiling.

From somewhere across the city, probably his imagination, he heard it: the Thornwood settling into evening. Tiny lights. Small animals. The deep old hum of an intact place.
